questions.question: What does the command 'pwd' stand for?

explanation.correct: pwd stands for Print Working Directory — it shows your current location in the filesystem.
explanation.why: A, C, D are incorrect. PWD is a standard POSIX command that outputs the absolute path of the current directory.

questions.question: Which command shows ALL files including hidden ones?

explanation.correct: ls -a shows all files including hidden files (those starting with a dot).
explanation.why: ls -l shows long format without hidden files. -h is human-readable sizes. --all-files is not a valid flag.

questions.question: In Linux, a hidden file is identified by:

options.text: A filename starting with a dot (.)
The file permissions being set to 000

explanation.correct: In Linux, any file or directory whose name starts with a dot (.) is considered hidden and not shown by default in ls.
explanation.why: There is no .hidden extension, permissions don't affect visibility, and there's no /hidden directory in Linux.

questions.question: What does 'cd ..' do?

options.text: Goes up one level to the parent directory

explanation.correct: cd .. moves you up one level to the parent directory. The .. always represents the parent directory in Linux.
explanation.why: cd / goes to root. cd ~ goes home. .. is a special directory reference, not a real folder named '..'.

questions.question: Which command creates nested directories in one go?

explanation.correct: mkdir -p creates the full path including all parent directories. The -p flag stands for 'parents'.
explanation.why: mkdir without -p would fail if projects or 2025 don't exist. -n and --nested are not valid mkdir flags.

questions.question: What command would you use to delete an empty directory?

explanation.correct: rmdir removes empty directories only. It fails with an error if the directory has any contents.
explanation.why: rm is for files (or rm -r for non-empty directories). del and remove are not standard Linux commands.

questions.question: What happens when you run 'rm file.txt' in Linux?

options.text: The file is moved to the Recycle Bin
The file is permanently deleted with no recovery
You are prompted to confirm before deletion
The file is renamed to file.txt.bak

explanation.correct: rm deletes files permanently. There is no Recycle Bin or Trash in the Linux CLI. The file is gone immediately.
explanation.why: Linux CLI has no Recycle Bin. rm without -i does not prompt. Files are not renamed. Recovery from rm requires backups or special forensic tools.

questions.question: Which character in the ls -l output indicates a directory?

explanation.correct: In ls -l output, the first character of each line indicates the file type. 'd' means directory.
explanation.why: '-' means regular file, 'l' means symlink, 'b' means block device. 'r' is part of permissions (read), not the type indicator.

questions.question: What does 'cat authorized_keys' do when run inside the .ssh directory?

options.text: Opens the file in a text editor
Displays the contents of the authorized_keys file in the terminal

explanation.correct: cat displays the contents of a file directly in the terminal. It does not open an editor or modify the file.
explanation.why: To edit, you'd use nano or vim. cat is read-only. rm would delete it. To create, you'd use touch or redirect output.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'history' command?

options.text: Shows all previously typed commands in the terminal
Shows the history of connected users

explanation.correct: history lists all commands you've typed in the terminal, numbered in order. It reads from the .bash_history file.
explanation.why: File modification history uses git or other version control. System boot history uses last or journalctl. User connection history uses last or who.

questions.question: What does the tilde (~) represent in a Linux file path?

explanation.correct: ~ is a shortcut for the current user's home directory. For ec2-user, ~ = /home/ec2-user.
explanation.why: Root directory is /. Hidden files start with dot (.). Previous directory is referenced with cd -.

questions.question: What does the $ sign at the end of the terminal prompt indicate?

options.text: You are logged in as root
You are logged in as a regular (non-root) user
The terminal is in interactive mode

explanation.correct: $ indicates a regular user. The root user's prompt ends with # instead.
explanation.why: Root always shows #. The $ has nothing to do with sudo requirements. It's a standard bash prompt indicator, not a mode indicator.

questions.question: You want to go from /home/ec2-user/projects/2025/January back to /home/ec2-user in one command. Which works?

explanation.correct: All three commands navigate to the home directory. cd with no argument, cd ~, and the absolute path all go to /home/ec2-user.
explanation.why: In bash, cd with no argument defaults to the home directory (same as cd ~). The absolute path always works. All three are valid.

questions.question: What is the difference between ls -l and ls -la?

options.text: ls -la includes hidden files (starting with dot) in the long-format listing
ls -la shows files in all subdirectories

explanation.correct: ls -la combines -l (long format) and -a (all files). It shows hidden files alongside regular files in full detail.
explanation.why: Neither flag filters by size. -a stands for 'all' not alphabetical (that's default anyway). To list subdirectories recursively, you'd use ls -R.

questions.question: You run 'mkdir projects/2025/January' but get 'No such file or directory'. Why?

options.text: mkdir cannot create directories with slashes in the name
The parent directories 'projects' or '2025' don't exist yet
You need sudo to create directories

explanation.correct: Without the -p flag, mkdir won't create parent directories if they don't exist. Add -p to create the entire path.
explanation.why: The error would be different if January existed. Slashes are path separators, not part of the name. Regular users can create directories in their home without sudo.

questions.question: rmdir fails with 'Directory not empty'. What should you use instead?

explanation.correct: rm -r recursively deletes a directory and all its contents. rmdir can only remove empty directories.
explanation.why: rmdir -f and rmdir --force are not valid flags. rm without -r would fail on a directory.

questions.question: What file stores your bash command history across sessions?

explanation.correct: Bash saves command history to ~/.bash_history (in your home directory). This file persists across terminal sessions.
explanation.why: /etc is for system-wide config, not user history. ~/.history is not the default. /var/log stores system logs, not user command history.

questions.question: Which command shows the last 5 commands from history?

explanation.correct: history followed by a number shows that many recent entries. 'history 5' shows the last 5 commands.
explanation.why: history -5 is not valid syntax. --last and 'last history' are not valid history options.

questions.question: What does 'cd ../../..' do from /home/ec2-user/projects/2025/January?

explanation.correct: From /home/ec2-user/projects/2025/January: one .. goes to 2025, two .. goes to projects, three .. goes to /home/ec2-user.
explanation.why: Count the levels: January→2025 (1), 2025→projects (2), projects→ec2-user (3). Three levels up from January lands at ec2-user.

questions.question: What does the -p flag in mkdir -p do if the directory already exists?

options.text: Silently skips creation — no error, no duplication

explanation.correct: With -p, mkdir silently does nothing if the directory already exists. This makes it safe for scripts — you can run it repeatedly without errors.
explanation.why: mkdir without -p would error if the directory exists. -p suppresses this error. It doesn't overwrite or prompt.

questions.question: A student on EC2 loses their .pem private key file. What is the recovery option?

options.text: Request AWS support to restore the key pair
Re-download the key from the EC2 console
Create a new EC2 instance — there is no recovery of the original

explanation.correct: AWS never stores your private key. Once lost, it cannot be recovered. You must create a new key pair and a new instance, or use EBS volume detach/reattach workaround.
explanation.why: AWS explicitly states they don't have your private key. The console shows the key pair name, not the key itself. recover-key is not a real command.

questions.question: What is the default username when SSHing into an Amazon Linux 2 EC2 instance?

explanation.correct: Amazon Linux 2 uses ec2-user as the default SSH username. Ubuntu instances use ubuntu, RHEL uses ec2-user or root.
explanation.why: Logging in as root directly is disabled by default on EC2. admin is used on some Debian-based AMIs. ubuntu is for Ubuntu AMIs only.

questions.question: What does 'ls -l' show that 'ls' alone does not?

options.text: File permissions, owner, size, and last modified date

explanation.correct: ls -l (long format) shows: file type, permissions (rwx), link count, owner, group, file size in bytes, and last modification timestamp.
explanation.why: Hidden files require -a. Recursive listing requires -R. ls -l shows both files and directories.

questions.question: PuTTY on Windows requires SSH keys in which format?

explanation.correct: PuTTY uses .ppk (PuTTY Private Key) format. AWS provides keys in .pem format which must be converted using PuTTYgen.
explanation.why: .pem is the AWS standard format but not compatible with PuTTY directly. .key and .cert are not standard SSH key formats for PuTTY.

questions.question: Which of the following paths is an ABSOLUTE path?

explanation.correct: An absolute path always starts with / (root). /home/ec2-user/projects is fully qualified from root and works from anywhere.
explanation.why: projects/2025 is relative (no leading /). ./projects is explicitly relative to current dir. ../reports is relative going up one level.

questions.question: What is the .ssh directory and where is it located on an EC2 instance?

options.text: A hidden directory at /home/ec2-user/.ssh containing SSH auth keys

explanation.correct: The .ssh directory in the user's home (/home/ec2-user/.ssh) stores SSH keys including authorized_keys which contains public keys allowed to connect.
explanation.why: /etc/ssh/ contains the SSH server daemon config (sshd_config), not user keys. /var/log/ssh doesn't exist by default. /usr/ssh is not a standard path.

questions.question: You run 'cat file1.txt file2.txt > combined.txt'. What does this do?

options.text: Displays file1 and file2 contents in the terminal
Merges file1 and file2 into a new file called combined.txt
Compares file1 and file2 for differences

explanation.correct: cat with multiple files concatenates them. The > operator redirects output to a new file instead of the terminal, creating combined.txt with both files' contents.
explanation.why: Without >, cat would print to terminal. >> would append to combined.txt if it existed. diff is the command to compare files.

questions.question: Which command re-runs command number 7 from your history?

explanation.correct: !N re-runs command number N from history. !7 runs whatever command was recorded as #7 in your history list.
explanation.why: 'history run 7', 'run 7', and 'exec 7' are not valid bash syntax for re-running history entries.

questions.question: A file shows '-rw-r--r--' in ls -l output. What type of file is it and who has write access?

options.text: Regular file; owner, group, and others

explanation.correct: The leading - means regular file. rw- is owner permissions (read+write). r-- is group (read only). r-- is others (read only). Only the owner has write permission.
explanation.why: d would indicate directory. l would indicate symlink. The second set r-- means group has read only, not write. Third set r-- means others have read only.

questions.question: What is the risk of running 'rm -rf /' on a Linux system?

options.text: It deletes all files in the current directory
It deletes the root folder name only
It recursively and forcefully deletes everything on the entire system starting from root
It resets the filesystem to factory defaults

explanation.correct: rm -rf / is one of the most destructive commands possible. -r means recursive (everything inside), -f means force (no prompts), / means start at root — meaning the entire filesystem.
explanation.why: This affects the ENTIRE system, not just the current directory. It doesn't 'reset' anything — it destroys. Modern Linux has a --no-preserve-root safeguard, but this should never be run.
